passage:
I'm Tenzin, and I supervise the second-year students in Dr Bose's lab. For three months Nirmala has been my easiest student. Extra data runs? "Yes, Tenzin, I'll do it." The outreach workshop, the poster, the department fest committee: yes, yes, yes. Each time I wrote "Excellent work!" on her reports, and each time she stood a little taller.
Last Friday I came in at seven and found her asleep over the bench, cheek on her notebook, a half-eaten biscuit beside her. She jolted up, laughing. "Just resting my eyes!"
I can't know what she's feeling. Most days she looks proud and lit up. But it struck me that every bit of praise I've given her has been about output. I've never once asked whether she still sings with the college choir, or when she last took a Sunday off.
This week I'm going to try asking.

qa.q: Where did Tenzin find Nirmala at seven last Friday?
qa.a: Asleep over the bench, cheek on her notebook, with a half-eaten biscuit beside her.

qa.q: What might Nirmala have been feeling when she jolted up laughing, 'Just resting my eyes!'?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed to be caught asleep and wanted to keep looking like the tireless student, though Tenzin can't be sure.

qa.q: What could Tenzin notice or praise from now on?
qa.a: Tenzin could ask about the choir and days off, and praise Nirmala for resting or turning something down, not only for results.

qa.q: What might it be like for Nirmala to hear only 'Excellent work!'?
qa.a: Nirmala may feel valued mostly when producing more, so saying yes keeps the praise coming even as her sleep runs short.

grounding: Shows a mentor noticing a proud student who says yes to everything and realising that praising only output has fed the overload.

passage:
Monday. Leela burst in waving her phone: elected class representative, picked for the college dance team, and a café wanting her to design their menu, paid. Her mother, Seema, hugged her. "That's my girl! Is there anything you can't do?" Leela beamed all through dinner.
Thursday, two weeks later. Seema woke at midnight to find Leela eating cold dal standing at the counter, laptop open to the menu. "Skipped dance," Leela said. "The rep meeting ran late." Her marks sheet lay on the table, all A grades. Seema began to say "Wonderful," then stopped. When had she last heard Leela laugh?
Sunday. Over tea, Seema tried a new question. "What did you actually enjoy this week?" Leela thought for a long time. "Nothing, really. Dance, maybe, when I went."
"Then maybe dance stays and something else goes. And I'm proud you slept till ten today."
Leela rolled her eyes, but she smiled.

qa.q: What three things did Leela announce on Monday?
qa.a: She was elected class representative, picked for the college dance team, and a café wanted her to design their menu, paid.

qa.q: Why did Seema stop herself from saying 'Wonderful' about the marks?
qa.a: Finding Leela eating cold dal at midnight worried her; she realised she couldn't remember Leela's last laugh, so praising marks suddenly felt wrong.

qa.q: Which of Seema's two responses helps more at this stage, and why?
qa.a: The Sunday one, asking what Leela enjoyed and praising her for sleeping in, because it values rest, limits and enjoyment rather than only results.

qa.q: What might Leela be feeling when her mother asks what she enjoyed?
qa.a: Leela may be caught off guard, noticing for the first time that almost nothing felt good that week, and a little relieved to be praised for resting.

grounding: Illustrates a parent who first praises a daughter's growing list of achievements, then notices the missing rest and joy and changes what she praises.

passage:
Sudha, you're proud of your student for taking on so much? Let me tell you about one of mine, years ago, when I still taught at the college.
Her name was Kavita. She said yes to everything: the magazine, the fest, two research projects, tutoring juniors. Every time she brought me a result, I praised it. "Brilliant, Kavita! What next?" I never once asked if she was sleeping. I never asked if she was enjoying any of it.
In her final term she came to my office and cried for an hour. She said, "I thought you'd be disappointed if I stopped."
That day I, Deepika, learned something. Praise the work, yes. But also ask, "Are you resting? Is this still fun?"

qa.q: What did Deepika say every time Kavita brought a result?
qa.a: "Brilliant, Kavita! What next?"

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when Kavita cried in her office?
qa.a: Deepika was shocked and regretful, realising the constant praise had pushed Kavita to keep saying yes.

qa.q: In the story, what could Deepika have done differently earlier?
qa.a: Asked about Kavita's sleep and enjoyment, not just praised each result, so Kavita felt free to set limits.

qa.q: What was Kavita experiencing through all those yeses?
qa.a: Kavita felt pressure to keep pleasing her teacher, fearing disappointment if she stopped.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how praising only a proud student's results rewarded overload, and learning to ask about rest and enjoyment.

passage:
Nitin had exactly ten minutes between lectures, and the corridor was packed with festival-week crowds. Zainab caught up with him, beaming.
"Sir, I've joined the cultural committee! And the hackathon team. And I'm still doing the research internship."
"That's wonderful," he began, then stopped. He'd said "wonderful" last month, too, when she took on the tutoring. He noticed the shadows under her eyes.
"Zainab, when did you last have a free evening?"
She laughed. "Free evening? What's that?"
"That's what worries me," Nitin said. "I'm proud of your work. I'd be just as proud if you said no to one of these."
She blinked, surprised. The bell rang.

qa.q: How many minutes did Nitin have between lectures?
qa.a: Exactly ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when he noticed the shadows under Zainab's eyes?
qa.a: He felt concerned, realising his praise might be rewarding her overload.

qa.q: What turning point does Nitin offer at this stage?
qa.a: He tells her he would be just as proud if she said no to something, valuing rest as much as output.

qa.q: What is it like for Zainab to hear this from her mentor?
qa.a: Zainab seems surprised, perhaps a little confused, since saying no had not seemed like something to be proud of.

grounding: Shows a mentor noticing a proud student saying yes to everything and choosing to value rest and limits, not only results.

passage:
Every Sunday at dinner in their Pune flat, Anand asked Manjula the same question: "So, what's new?" And every Sunday she had something: a prize, a new club, a leadership role.
"My daughter," he'd tell his friends. "She can do anything."
This Sunday she listed four things, talking fast, and yawned in the middle of a sentence. She hadn't touched her guitar in weeks.
Anand put down his fork. He thought of how often he'd said "What next?" and how rarely he'd asked anything else.
"Manju, forget new things. What did you enjoy this week? When did you last just sit?"
Manjula stared at him, fork halfway to her mouth, as if nobody had asked that before.

qa.q: What question did Anand ask every Sunday?
qa.a: "So, what's new?"

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when he put down his fork?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and a little guilty, noticing his praise had only ever asked about achievements.

qa.q: Why is Anand's new question a helpful turning point?
qa.a: It shows Manjula that enjoyment and rest matter to him too, not just output.

qa.q: What is it like for Manjula to be asked what she enjoyed?
qa.a: Manjula seems surprised and unsettled, as if nobody had asked her that before.

grounding: Shows a father who has praised only his proud daughter's achievements noticing her overload and asking about rest and enjoyment.

passage:
"Papa, I got picked for the hackathon team too!" Aadhya dropped her bag by the door.
"Wah! That's my girl," Samir said, looking up from the newspaper. "The research internship, the college magazine, and now this?"
"And I said yes to the fest committee. They said nobody else could handle sponsorship."
"Of course they did." He smiled, then paused. "When did you last sleep before one?"
"Papa, sleep is for after placements." She laughed and opened the fridge. "Is there any of that leftover pulao?"
"You ate standing up yesterday also."
"Because I had a call at eight."
Samir folded the paper slowly. "Beta, I keep saying well done for everything you finish. I don't think I've once asked if you're enjoying any of it."
Aadhya closed the fridge. "Some of it."
"Which part? Tell me that part."

qa.q: Which committee did Aadhya say yes to?
qa.a: The fest committee, to handle sponsorship.

qa.q: What does Samir's slow folding of the newspaper suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He is growing uneasy and concerned, realising his praise may have been rewarding her overload.

qa.q: What shift in Samir's praise could help Aadhya?
qa.a: Asking what she enjoys and noticing her rest and limits, not only congratulating each new result.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel when Samir asks which part she enjoys?
qa.a: She pauses, perhaps caught off guard and a little relieved to be asked about enjoyment instead of results.

grounding: Shows a parent praising a proud student's growing list of commitments, then noticing that praise for output alone rewards overload.
